title: Headings & Paragraphs
summary: Headings organize a page, and paragraphs hold related sentences.

subtopics.title: The document frame
subtopics.explanation: `<h1>` is usually the main heading that describes the page. It helps readers understand what the page is about. It is like the title on a book cover. A page can have more than one heading in some structures, but keep the outline clear and make the main subject easy to find. In practice, a recipe page can use one main heading, then headings for ingredients and steps. In practice, write a heading that names the section rather than repeating a generic label.

subtopics.title: Important pieces
subtopics.explanation: `<h2>` introduces a major section under the page’s main heading. It is like a chapter title under the book title. Use it when the content begins a new major part, not merely to make text large. A screen reader can use headings to jump through a page. In practice, a screen reader can list the page headings so someone can jump to a section. In practice, a paragraph can contain inline links or emphasis while preserving one text idea.

subtopics.title: Page information
subtopics.explanation: `<h3>` introduces a subsection within a larger section. It is like a section label inside a chapter. Do not skip levels only to get a smaller visual size; choose the level that matches the content outline. Then style the heading with CSS if its appearance needs adjustment. In practice, a heading’s visual size belongs in CSS; its level belongs to the outline. In practice, use CSS margins to set paragraph spacing instead of empty paragraphs.

subtopics.title: Content structure
subtopics.explanation:
`

` marks a paragraph of related sentences. It gives the browser a meaningful text block and creates default spacing. It is like grouping sentences on one note card. Use paragraphs for prose rather than adding line breaks after every sentence, which makes the document harder to edit and understand. In practice, split a long explanation into paragraphs when the subject or point changes. In practice, a visual design can restyle h2 and h3 while keeping their hierarchy intact.

subtopics.title: Good habits
subtopics.explanation: Use headings to describe the structure, not as decoration. Keep their order logical and write labels that predict the content below. This is like an outline that helps readers find a chapter before they open the book. Change font size, weight, and spacing in CSS while preserving the heading meaning. In practice, test the outline with CSS disabled to see whether the structure still makes sense. In practice, review the heading list with a screen reader or browser accessibility tool.

foundations.overview: Headings and paragraphs give a page a readable outline. A heading names the section that follows; a paragraph groups sentences about one idea. Think of headings as chapter labels in a book. Use heading levels in a sensible order for the content, not because a particular size looks attractive. CSS controls appearance while HTML communicates structure.
foundations.whyItMatters: A readable page outline helps visitors scan and helps assistive technology offer quick navigation. Meaningful paragraphs also make content easier to edit and translate.
commonUseCases: Use headings to divide a help article into scan-friendly sections.
Use paragraphs for related sentences in a description.
Keep heading levels logical so a screen-reader user can navigate the outline.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A heading is just large bold text.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Heading elements create navigable structure and should reflect the content outline.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Choose h2 or h3 based on the font size you want.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Choose the level by hierarchy, then style its size with CSS.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A paragraph tag is needed after every line break.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Paragraphs group related sentences; line breaks serve a different purpose and should not replace document structure.

visualExplorer.title: Building a document outline
visualExplorer.caption: Headings form a nested outline. Start with one h1, then descend level by level without skipping — exactly how assistive tech reads the page.

config.intro: A well-structured page reads like a table of contents. Follow these steps to build a clean heading outline.

steps.name: One h1 for the page
steps.detail: Give the page a single h1 describing its main subject — the title at the top of the outline.

steps.name: h2 for top sections
steps.detail: Each major section of the page gets an h2, sitting directly under the h1 in the outline.

steps.name: h3 nested under h2
steps.detail: Subsections of an h2 use h3. Never jump from h2 straight to h4 — that skips a level.

steps.name: Paragraphs fill the sections
steps.detail:
Within each section, write running text as

elements, one idea per paragraph.

steps.name: Style with CSS, not levels
steps.detail: If an h3 needs to look bigger, set its font-size in CSS — don't promote it to an h2.

interactiveExamples.title: A clean heading outline with paragraphs
interactiveExamples.explanation: One h1 for the page title, h2s for sections, and paragraphs for prose. The browser supplies the spacing automatically.

keyTakeaways: `<h1>` is usually the main heading that describes the page.
`<h2>` introduces a major section under the page’s main heading.
`<h3>` introduces a subsection within a larger section.

`

` marks a paragraph of related sentences.
Use headings to describe the structure, not as decoration.
